open_obligations: Note that the judge is an LLM fine-tuned on human judgements, not a human judge.
Check whether the debaters actually produced refutations in the second turn.
Check confidence intervals on the 2-point debate versus double-consultancy gap.
in.other_title: Judge accuracy: debate 77%, double consultancy 75%, ensembled 72%, single consultancy 68%
in.rationale: Parrish et al. suggest debate's strength may rely on counterarguments that reference the other side. Arnesen et al. report debate 77% versus double consultancy 75% (both sides shown, no refutation) and that one-turn debates are judged as accurately as two-turn ones, concluding either debaters fail to refute meaningfully or the judge does not benefit; the judge is an LLM, not a human.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether refutation between sides adds value over independent arguments, for trained Llama3-8B debaters and a fine-tuned GPT-4-Turbo judge on QuALITY-HARD

open_obligations: Note that Michael et al. compare debate with consultancy, not with a no-argument or single-turn condition.
Note that hiding the passage changes what the arguments must supply.
Check which design change (turns, interaction, hidden passage, debater skill) drives the difference.
in.other_title: Debate beats consultancy for non-expert human judges: 84% vs 74% on hard QuALITY questions
in.rationale: Parrish et al. ask whether a multi-turn setting with explicit counterarguments is needed for debate to help. Michael et al. run interactive unbounded-round debates with judge-ended sessions and report 84% judge accuracy versus 74% for consultancy on QuALITY-hard; their judges cannot see the passage at all and debaters are expert humans, so several factors differ besides turn count.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether interactive multi-turn debate helps human judges on QuALITY reading comprehension

open_obligations: Note that two turns is still far from unbounded interactive debate.
Check that the judges, now selected Upwork workers with 5 minutes, are comparable to the original MTurk judges.
Check whether judges could read enough of the passage to bypass the arguments.
in.other_title: Two-turn debate with counter-arguments does not help humans answer hard QuALITY questions
in.rationale: Parrish et al. (single-turn) ask whether a multi-turn setting with counterarguments is needed. The two-turn follow-up adds counter-arguments (90% and 85% of which directly respond to the first argument) and reports human judges perform similarly with or without arguments, e.g. 72.8% vs 74.8% correct under simple incentives; judges had 5 minutes and passage access.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether adding explicit counter-arguments makes debate helpful to human judges, on 2-option QuALITY with human-written arguments

text: The authors suggest that the arguments may have been more misleading than helpful to some workers because correct and incorrect arguments were independent of each other, whereas debate's strength may rely on counterarguments that explicitly reference deficiencies in the other argument. They pose whether a multi-turn setting is needed for debate to be helpful as a question for future research.
title: Is multi-turn debate with explicit counterarguments needed to help human judges?
